about: The words of the chain dirham_hoard (Data/encounters/chain_dirham_hoard_793.json; Design/content/chains/dirham_hoard.md): a dying Gotlander's account of silver buried on his farm, and the kin who also know. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the news items its endings post; and an 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. Nobody says 'dirham': it is the writing silver, the Saracens' silver. Nothing here is quoted from any book: all of it is our own wording (the verse at the pyre is given as the text havamal_077, not written out here). Hegbjorn, Vivil, Ailikn, Ottar, the boy Liknat and the rower Torkel are invented. Gotlanders say the number first and the feeling never. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: A man with no kin in harbour

A Gotland trader lies sick of a fever in a host's back room. His ship went east without him nine days ago; a ship does not wait on one man's fever. He has asked the host to find him a man with a boat of his own, who is not of his island and not a Svea. The host found you.
He pays, so he lies here. But he will not see the new moon, and he knows it. He has been asking for a stranger with a boat since yesterday. I do not know why a stranger.
Hegbjorn. Of Gotland. Sit where I can see your hands. A stranger is better: he has no cousin of mine to please.
My farm is Aikgard, half a morning in from the beach at Paviken. Thirty summers I went east for the writing silver. I did not bring it home to look at.
The storehouse with the stone footing. Stand at the south door post. Walk toward the tall stone with the ship cut on it. Twelve feet. Under the boards, a flat slab.
My brother Vivil holds the farm and knows there is silver in it. My daughter Ailikn knows I once walked her to a stone. Neither knows the feet. Vivil would only bury it deeper.
Forty marks, less one, in all. Carry the word to Ailikn. A third is the bringer's, that is the custom. Give me your hand on it and I will tell you the rest.
Give him your hand on it: his daughter shall have the word
Promise nothing, and pay the host for a bed by the fire and someone to sit with him
Hear him out and promise nothing

His hand is hot and dry and stronger than it looks. He does not let go until he has finished. 'In the east pasture old stones stand in the shape of a ship. The stern stone is the tallest. On its seaward side, an arm deep. That is the greater part, and no one alive knows it but you.' Then he asks for water and turns his face to the wall.

The host takes the pennies and moves him to the bench by the hearth, and his wife's mother sits down beside him with her spinning. The Gotlander watches you pay. 'So. You would not swear, and you paid. I have known men who did it the other way.' He says no more about silver.
You hear him to the end and give him nothing but a nod. He looks at you for a long time. 'Twelve feet,' he says again, 'toward the stone.' Whatever else he had to say, he keeps.
What he left

The Gotlander died in the night. The host has laid him in the outhouse and put his sea chest on the table: a folding scale in a bronze case, a bag of weights, a comb, and a stick of yew cut with runes on two sides. He wants his lodging paid and the room back.
He went before cockcrow, quietly. He asked what the wind was. I told him west. He said that was no use to him.
My wife's mother sat with him to the end, as you paid for. He gave her the stick to hold and then took it back.
Eight pennies for the bed and the broth. The chest covers it if nobody pays. A scale like that sells. The stick I would burn.
One of his own rowers was here last night, a Svea, off a boat that came back. He stood in my door and asked what the old man had said to the Frisian. I said I do not listen at sickbeds.
His people burn their dead, I am told. Wood costs. Otherwise he goes in the sand above the tide line with the other strangers.
Pay his lodging and the wood, burn him as his people do, and take the chest for his kin
Pay his lodging, take the chest for his kin, and leave the body to the host
Leave the chest for the lodging. You carry his words, and that is enough

The fire is lit on the shore at dusk, with the wind off the land. A Northman from the next berth comes and stands by it unasked, and says a verse his people say over the dead, the one about what does not die. Afterwards he says it again slowly so that you have it. You put the scale, the weights and the yew stick in your own chest. The host says he has seen kin do less.

The host counts the pennies twice and slides the chest across the table. The scale folds into a case no bigger than your palm. The stick is cut on two sides with runes and worn smooth where a thumb held it. They put him in the sand that afternoon. You are not there.

The host shrugs and carries the chest to the back. By evening a Dane has bought the scale. The stick goes with the comb for a cup of ale, to a man the host does not know. You have the dead man's words and nothing of his to show for them.
A stick of yew

The dead man's stick lies on the thwart beside his scale. It is a hand long, cut on two sides with runes, and worn smooth where a thumb has held it. Two of your men have seen it and have things to say.
I can read that. It is no great boast, mind. Any man from north of the Eider can. Look how he cut it. Deep, and without haste. A man does not cut a market tally that deep.
It is a dead man's word to his child. That is a debt, and we are carrying it. I would no more read it than open another man's purse.
Where I come from they say a man has in the next place what he put in the ground himself. Dig it up and you have made him poor. I forget who told it to me. I only say what they say.
Then he would not have told anyone the feet. He told. He wanted it dug.
Have it read aloud, before every man aboard
Spell it out yourself, at night, by the steering oar
Wrap it in the scale's cloth and carry it to his kin unread

He turns it to the light and reads with his thumb, a rune at a time. 'Stern stone. Sea side. Arm deep. Hegbjorn cut this.' Nobody says anything. Then the steersman says, 'Well. Now it is four men's secret, and that is safer than one man's.' He may be right.

Sixteen signs, and some of them do for three sounds. It takes you most of two night watches and a great deal of muttering. Stern. Stone. Sea. Side. Arm. Deep. And a name. You wrap the stick again before the watch changes.

Sixteen signs, and some of them do for three sounds. By the end of the watch you have 'stone' and what may be 'arm' or 'eagle', and a sore head. You know more runes than you did. You do not know what he cut.

You fold the stick into the cloth with the scale and put both at the bottom of your chest. The Northman lifts one shoulder. The Frisian, who has been watching your hands, goes back to his steering and looks easier than he did.
Asking on the beach

Paviken is a beach, a row of boat sheds and the smoke of forges. There is no wall and no reeve, and nobody asks what you carry. You ask a shipwright for the farm called Aikgard. He puts down his adze before he answers, which is not a good sign.
Hegbjorn's. So he is dead. A man does not send a Frisian to ask the way to his own gate.
Follow the stream up to the second ford and keep the ridge on your left hand. His brother Vivil holds the farm. A careful man. He has not sold a sheep he could keep in twenty years.
The daughter is Ailikn. Widowed two winters, one small boy. She lives with her mother's people, the farm with the three ash trees, nearer the shore. She does not ask her uncle for anything.
You are the second this moon. A Svea who rowed for Hegbjorn came off a boat and asked the same. He went up the stream and came down again the same day, not pleased.
Whichever gate you knock at first, the other will hear of it before night. It is not a large island.
Go to the farm and the brother first, as a guest should
Go to the daughter first, as the dead man asked
Stay a day on the beach, buy the wrights ale, and learn how Gotlanders inherit
You take the stream path in the morning. At the second ford a boy with a dog watches you cross and then runs, not toward Aikgard but toward the shore, where three ash trees stand over a roof.

The farm with the three ash trees is small and well kept. A woman of about twenty-five hears you out at the gate without asking you in, then fetches her cloak. 'We will go to my uncle's together. I will not have him say I heard it behind his back.'

Ale loosens shipwrights. A farm here is not cut up: brothers hold it together and the eldest speaks for it. Sons take after the father; where there are no sons, the daughter. Land does not leave the kin. Silver a man earned himself, abroad, is another matter, and they argue about it until the cask is empty. They also say, twice, that no one on this beach has tasted Rhine wine since last summer.
Aikgard

The farm lies half a morning in from the beach: a long house, a storehouse on a stone footing, sheep on thin grass over limestone, and a tall stone by the gate with a ship cut on it. Vivil sets ale and bread before you and asks nothing until you have eaten. Ailikn has walked over from her mother's people and sits by the door with her boy.
Eat first. A man who has come over the sea to my table can tell me my brother is dead when he has had bread.
He came to my gate before yours, uncle. I brought him here myself. Count that for me or against me as you like.
He came to the house first, as is right. I sent for you, niece, within the hour. Nobody will say I did not.
That is his scale. He let me hold the pans when I was small, and I was not to breathe on them.
Thirty summers he went east and I kept his fields with mine. What he brought home he ate at my table and laid under my roofs. It is the farm's silver.
He had one child. He rowed for that silver, uncle; you did not. If he sent a word over the sea, he sent it to someone.
You have been drinking with the wrights, I hear, and know our law now. Then you know that the farm is not divided. Whether a bowl of silver is the farm is what they could not tell you.
Ask the daughter to walk with you to the gate, and tell her alone
Tell the brother, who holds the farm and set the bread before you
Say it once, aloud, to both of them, and let them call neighbours to hear it

At the gate, under the stone with the ship on it, you tell her: the south door post, toward this stone, twelve feet, a slab. She looks at the storehouse and then at the house, where her uncle stands in the door. 'It is under his roof,' she says. 'So I shall have to dig it in front of him.' She does not sound sorry.

Vivil hears it with his eyes on the table. Then he gets up, walks to the storehouse door and stands looking at the floor. Ailikn takes her boy by the hand and goes without a word to anyone. When you leave, Vivil gives you a bundle of fleeces, because a guest is not sent off empty.

Vivil sends a boy to the two nearest farms, and you say it standing, before six people: the south door post, toward the tall stone, twelve feet, a slab under the boards. Nobody moves toward the storehouse. 'The day after tomorrow,' Vivil says, 'in daylight, with these same men.' Ailikn nods. It is the first thing they have agreed on. She brings you a crock of honey when you go.
Under the floor

The storehouse boards are up. Twelve feet from the south door post, toward the tall stone, there is a flat slab, and under the slab a bronze bowl with a wooden lid. Arm rings. Twisted rods. A bag of thin coins with writing on them and no face, many cut in half. It is a great deal of silver. It is not what he spoke of.
Fifteen marks, near enough. At my table, two winters back, he said forty less one. My brother did not say forty when he meant fifteen.
Nor did he keep all his eggs under one hen. He told me that often enough.
You told her and not me, Frisian, on my own ground. I do not forget it. But it came out of my floor, and it stays in my house until better men than us have spoken.
You told him and not me. He would have had it up by night if the neighbours had not seen you come. It was my father's hand that filled that bowl.
The thing meets when the hay is in. Until then the bowl stands on the cross beam, where all can see it and none can reach it without a ladder.
And you, Frisian, will be asked what he said. All of it. Be on the island.
Set up a scale on the door slab and call out every weight for both to hear
Ask for an earnest now, against the share of the man who brought the word
Stand in the door and ask for nothing yet

Ring by ring and bag by bag, with the beam level each time before you speak. Fifteen marks and three ounces. Vivil cuts a notch for each mark on one stick and Ailikn on another, and at the end they lay the sticks side by side. Then each of them puts an ounce in your pan, for the weighing, and neither looks at the other while doing it.

You say it plainly: the bringer's share is the custom, and you have a crew to feed. Vivil looks at Ailikn. Ailikn looks at the bowl. 'A mark and five ounces on account,' Vivil says, 'out of whichever of us wins.' He weighs it himself and is not mean with the beam.

You say it plainly, and it is the wrong morning for plain speaking. 'The hole is not cold,' Vivil says. He weighs out six ounces, with his thumb nowhere near the pan and his face like the slab. Ailikn says nothing at all.

You stand in the door and keep your hands in your belt. When the bowl is on the cross beam and the boards are down, Vivil walks you to the gate and puts two cakes of wax in your arms. 'For the house's candles,' he says, though his own house burns tallow. Ailikn sees it and, for once, seems to think well of him.
Six oars

A six-oared boat has come out from behind a skerry and lies across your bow. No sail, no cargo, six men, and the oars held level. The one in the stern stands up. You have heard of him twice already: in a host's doorway, and on the beach at Paviken.
Frisian! Torkel is my name. Six summers at Hegbjorn's third oar. You sat by his bed. I stood in the door, where rowers stand.
He paid his men when the ship came home. He did not come home. I am owed half a mark, and his brother set a dog on me for asking.
So. You went up to his farm and you came down again. What rides under your deck boards?
Pay him what the dead man owed him: half a mark, weighed over the gunwale
Heave to, lift the deck boards, and tell him who has the silver
Put her before the wind. Six oars tire; a sail does not

You weigh it on the dead man's kind of scale, with both boats rising and falling, and it takes three tries. Torkel bites one piece, laughs at himself and puts it away. 'Six summers, and a Frisian pays me. If they ask at the thing what he said in that room, send for me. I heard him name the girl.' The six oars back water and let you by.

You lift the boards yourself. He looks at wine, wool and bilge water for some time. 'On a cross beam,' he says, when you tell him. 'Under the brother's roof. Then I will never see an ounce of it.' He sits down. The boat pulls away slowly, like men going home from a bad market.

You lift the boards. Two of his men come over the gunwale anyway and go through the hold with their hands. They find no bowl. They find your purse, and Torkel takes out of it what he says he is owed, less than he says, and gives the purse back. 'Now we are even, you and the dead man and I.' It is one way of counting.

The sail fills and she heels and goes. They row hard for the length of ten ship's lengths and gain, and then for another ten and do not, and then the oars come up one after another. Torkel is still standing in the stern when you lose him against the skerries. He will know your sail again.

The wind drops under the land just as the sail fills. For a while it is six oars against a slack sheet, and they come close enough to throw. A stone the size of a loaf takes one of your men on the shoulder before the breeze comes back. Nobody is laughing when you clear the point.
The only witness

The hay is in and the thing has met on the slope above the farms: sixty free men sitting on the grass, their spears stuck upright behind them. The bronze bowl stands on a hide in the middle of the ring. Vivil stands on one side of it and Ailikn on the other. An old man who knows the law by heart asks who heard the dead man speak, and every head turns to the Frisian.
We have no king here to ask, and we do not want one. We have what was said and who heard it. You heard it. Stand where all can see you.
The farm is one. My brother and I never divided it. What lay under the farm's floor is the farm's, and I speak for the farm.
My father had no son. What a man earns with his own oar goes to his own child. My uncle has had thirty summers of my father's fields. I ask only for my father's silver.
I rowed for him six summers and stood in the door of that room. I am a Svea and nobody's cousin here. I heard him say his daughter's name. More I did not hear.
A stranger's word weighs what the stranger weighs. Say less than you heard and we shall know it by winter. It is not a large island.
Say his words as he said them, the hard ones too
Say he named his daughter and no one else
Say he spoke of the farm's silver, and the farm is Vivil's

You say all of it: that he named the farm his, that he said his brother held it, that he said to carry the word to his daughter, and that he said Vivil would only bury it deeper. There is some laughter at that, and Vivil goes red and then, slowly, almost smiles. The old man speaks with four others and comes back. Ten marks to the child. Five to the farm that kept it. Three ounces to the stranger, 'who said a thing that did him no good with either side'.

You say he named his daughter, and you stop there. The old man waits a while to see if there is more. There is not. All fifteen marks go to Ailikn, who pays you two ounces before the whole ring. Vivil pulls his spear out of the turf and walks home without waiting for the other cases.

You say he spoke of the farm's silver, in the farm's storehouse, and you stop there. The old man looks at you for longer than is comfortable. All fifteen marks go to the farm. Vivil weighs you out a mark that evening, generously, and Ailikn passes you on the path as if you were a fence post.
Fifteen of forty

The evening after the thing. Fifteen marks came out of the floor, and at this table two winters ago the dead man spoke of forty less one. In the east pasture, a bowshot beyond the fence, old stones stand in the shape of a ship, bow to the sea. Sheep graze between them. Nobody at the table looks that way, because nobody at the table has any reason to.
Four and twenty marks. That is the weight of a grown man's life on this island, in silver, and it is lying somewhere on my land laughing at me.
He walked me to a stone once, when I was six, and said, remember this stone. I have tried every stone on the farm since. There are a great many stones on this farm.
If it were mine I would not put it back under anything. Twenty-four marks is a ship of sixteen paces with her sail, and a cargo to fill her. Silver in a hole does not have young.
Silver in a hole does not sink either, boy. Ask on the beach how many ships came home last summer and how many went out.
Frisian. You have told us what he said about the floor. Was the floor all he said?
Tell Ailikn where the rest lies, and her alone
Tell Vivil where the rest lies: it is his pasture
Say it at the table, to all three, and say what you would do with such silver
Say you know of no more than the floor, and walk out to look at the evening

You find her at the well after dark and say it, or put the yew stick in her hand and let her read it with her thumb. The stern stone. The seaward side. An arm deep. She is quiet for a moment. 'That stone. I sat on that stone to eat my bread.' Then: 'The night after tomorrow, before light. Bring two men who do not talk.'

You walk the fence with Vivil at dusk and say it, or give him the yew stick and let him read it. He looks out at the stones for some time. 'Under my own sheep,' he says. 'Thirty summers.' He does not ask you to help him dig. He asks you to stay away from the east pasture until he sends for you.

You say it at the table: the stern stone, the seaward side, an arm deep. Then, before anyone can stand up, you say the rest: that it has been in a hole for years and done nothing; that Ottar wants a ship and Paviken builds them; that you can fill her with what the east wants and sell what she brings back on the Rhine. Three shares. It is quiet for a long time. 'He believed him at the thing,' Ailikn says at last, to her uncle. 'So did you.' Vivil says he will sleep on it. He does not say no, and on this island that is a great deal.

You say the floor was all you can tell them. Ailikn looks at you a moment longer than the others. Then the talk turns to the hay. You go out, and your feet take you along the fence toward the east pasture, where the old stones are black against the last of the light.
Her father's daughter

Before light, at the stern stone, on the seaward side, an arm deep: a second bowl, bigger than the first, sealed with pitch. Ailikn has your scale set up on a fallen stone beside it before the sun is over the trees. Her uncle stands at the pasture fence and comes no nearer.
Twenty-four marks and an ounce over. He was never out by more than an ounce in his life.
There is a shore strip next to my mother's people that has wanted a buyer since the winter. And a half share in a ship at Paviken. My son will not row at another man's oar.
On my land! Under my sheep! Thirty summers I kept his fields!
A third is the bringer's. Eight marks. I have weighed it twice; weigh it again yourself. And my storehouse is dry, and nearer the beach than his. Leave what you like in it.
Take the third she weighs out: eight marks
Take four marks and furs from his store, and ask her to carry the other four to the fence herself

Eight marks, in rings and cut coin, weighed three times in all. Your men carry it down to the boat in two bags. Ailikn buys the shore strip before the first frost and her half of a ship before the second. She keeps a corner of her storehouse for the Frisian house from that day. Vivil does not come to the launching. He is said to have dug over half the east pasture that autumn and found a dead sheep.

She looks at you as her father must have looked at a bad bargain. Then she takes four marks in her apron and walks to the fence, and you do not hear what is said there. It takes a long time. When she comes back Vivil is with her, carrying nothing, and he gives you his hand, and says that a man who throws away four marks to mend another family's fence may tie up at Paviken any winter he likes and name Aikgard to whoever asks. She adds two timbers of marten from her father's own store, 'so that nobody says a daughter of Hegbjorn's paid short'.
The farm's silver

Vivil dug alone, at night, and would not have a lamp. In the morning there is a pitch-sealed bowl on his table and fresh turf at the stern stone. He has weighed out five marks for you. The rest he has already carried out of the house, and he has earth on his knees again.
Five marks. A third is for the man who finds. You did not find; you carried. Five is fair for carrying, and I have added wax.
The rest is where a bad year can find it and nobody else can. Not under that stone. I am not a fool. My son will be told when I am as sick as my brother was.
The farm has a strip of shore north of the wrights' sheds. Twenty paces of it are yours, for a boathouse, while your house keeps coming. I will say so before neighbours.
My niece has ten marks of the floor by the thing's own word, or she has nothing by it. Either way the thing has spoken. I owe her a place at my table. I have never denied her that.
Take the five marks, the wax and the shore strip, and ask no more
Take them, and say across his table that a brother's child is owed a marriage portion from it

Five marks, three cakes of wax, and twenty paces of shingle marked with four stones before two neighbours. It is a good morning's pay. On the stream path you meet Ailikn coming up with her boy. She has heard; everyone has. She steps off the path to let you pass and does not answer your greeting. Vivil lives eleven more winters. Whether he was ever as sick as his brother, and whom he told, nobody on the beach can say.

He goes red to the ears. He says a Frisian might mind his own fence. Then he says nothing for the time it takes to drink a horn of ale. Then he gets up, goes out, comes back with earth on his knees for the third time that day, and puts two marks on the table. 'For when she marries again. Not before. Tell her it was my thought.' You tell her it was his thought. She does not believe it, and takes it.

He hears you to the end. 'You have your five marks and your shingle,' he says. 'Do not make me weigh them again.' The neighbours look at the rafters. You take what is yours and go. On the stream path Ailikn steps aside for you and does not answer your greeting.
The stern stone

The ship of stones lies in the east pasture with its bow to the sea, as it has lain longer than anyone can say. The stern stone is the tallest and leans a little. The turf on its seaward side has not been cut in years. From here you can see the farm's smoke, and nobody can see you.
Stern stone, sea side, arm deep. That is this one. We are standing on four and twenty marks, and the only two men who ever knew it are you and a man who is ash now.

Forty less one, he said, and fifteen came up. I am slow at sums, but even I can do that one. The rest is somewhere under this island. So is a great deal else, they tell me. Good stones, these. Somebody meant them.
Before you say anything, hear me. He keeps two dogs. Two. The nights are short at this time of year, and a stranger found digging here is not asked his reasons. I only count what I see.
You walk a long way to look at old stones, Frisian. My father did the same, the night before he sailed. I never knew what he saw in them.
My uncle and I have agreed on one thing this year. Five marks from the floor are yours, for the carrying. And this ring, whole. He wore it. Do not cut it.
Lay your hand on the stone, and go down to the boat
Leave it, and give the yew stick to her small son, to keep until he can read it
Send to the boat for the spade and two men, and wait for dark

The stone is warm from the day. You take your hand away and go down to the boat with five marks and a dead man's arm ring, and you do not look back at the pasture more than twice. The sheep graze there for as long as there are sheep at Aikgard. Whatever lies under the stern stone lies there still, an arm deep, on the seaward side.

The boy is four. He takes the stick in both hands and looks at the cuts. 'It is your grandfather's,' you say. 'When you can read it, read it by yourself.' Ailikn starts to speak and does not. At the gate she says, 'Any winter you are caught in these waters, the three ash trees. And my uncle says the same of Aikgard, though he will say it worse.' The boy is already trying the stick against every stone in the yard.
You send a man down the stream path for the spade. It is a long evening. The light goes slowly at this time of year, and the stones seem to stand closer together as it goes.
An arm deep

No moon. The spade goes in on the seaward side of the stern stone, and an arm down it rings on bronze. The bowl is sealed with pitch and takes two men to lift. Up at the farm a dog has started, stopped, and started again.
Careful with it. That is the weight of a grown ewe. So it is two men, and slowly, or one bag at a time and three goings. I cannot make it less. It is a long way to the beach either way.
That dog has our wind. Hear him. If he is loosed we are four strangers in a field with a spade. I have been found in better company, and I would sooner not be found in this.
You gave the old man your hand, I think. Yes. You did. I say nothing. I only remember it, so that one of us does.
It is yours to say, not mine. All of it, some of it, or none. But choose quickly. The hole is the only thing here that will not be missed by morning.
Take all of it and be at sea by first light
Take a finder's third, eight marks and one ring, and lay the turf back over the rest
Look at it, seal it again, and fill the hole

Two men on the bowl and two ahead, down the stream bed where the dogs cannot follow a scent. You are afloat before the east is grey. Nineteen marks and more, once the pitch is off, and a twisted neck ring as thick as a thumb that every smith in the north would know. By noon there is a hole at Aikgard and a spade-cut turf, and by evening the whole island knows who walked out to the stones. Do not winter on Gotland.

The dog is loosed while the bowl is still at the fence. It goes over, the lid goes, and four and twenty marks go into the long grass in the dark. You get one bag to the boat, and a man with a torn leg, and a twisted neck ring somebody had the wit to put on his own arm. Behind you there are torches in the east pasture. Vivil will have the rest picked out of the grass by sunrise, and he will know to an ounce what is missing.

You weigh eight marks by feel and a lamp held under a cloak, take one twisted ring for the trouble, and press the pitch back with your thumbs. The turf goes down in the order it came up. By morning the dew has closed over it. Sixteen marks lie there yet. Nobody on the island knows. Three of your men do, and you will hear of it some night when the ale is strong and the pay is late.

You lift the lid a hand's breadth. Rings, coiled one inside another like sleeping snakes, and the thin coins poured over them. You look for as long as it takes to say a short prayer, and then you seal it and fill the hole and tread the turf. In the morning Vivil and Ailikn weigh you five marks for the carrying, and Ailikn gives you her father's arm ring, whole. They think you look tired. The dog knows you and is quiet.
Silver that floats

A new ship lies on the beach at Paviken, home from the east three days, her sail of chequered wool spread on the shingle to dry. Skins are stacked in a new booth above the tide line, and the booth has a Frisian's mark cut over the door. Ottar, Ailikn and Vivil are waiting by the scale. Nobody has dug anything on Aikgard this year except a well.
Out by the long island, in over the lake, back before the first night frost. One man lost to a fever, none to the sea. Your wine went for twice its weight in skins. I should have taken more.

Thirty-nine marks went into her keel, her sail and her cargo. She has brought home more than twice that in skins, wax and silver, and she still floats. I have weighed it three times. A hole never did that.
A ship can sink. I said so and I say so. But I have counted it too, and I will leave the farm's share in her one more summer. One.
A third of the gain is yours, as we said at my father's table. And the booth, while you keep coming. Give me your hand on next summer and I will sail with your goods under my own.

Nine marks of silver and a little over, a timber of sable, two of marten, three cakes of wax, and Ottar's hand, which is as hard as his uncle's was and a good deal cooler. Ailikn cuts three notches in the booth's door post, one for each share. Vivil watches her do it and says the post was sound before. Next spring the ship goes east with Rhine wine under her boards and a Frisian tally stick beside the Gotland one.

You take the sable and two and a half marks to pay your men, and leave the rest in her. Ottar is so pleased that he forgets to be a Gotlander about it. Vivil gives you a long look, the look of a man who has found another fool to share his risk, and then, for the first time, sets ale before you without being the host.

Twelve and a half marks, weighed out on the shingle. Ottar is sorry and does not hide it. Ailikn says only that the booth is yours while you keep coming, since that was said at the table, and that a third share in the ship will not be hard to sell on this beach now that people have seen her come home.
On Gotland they say Hegbjorn of Aikgard's silver was under an old stone all the time, and that his daughter had it up before her uncle was awake. She has bought shore and half a ship.
On Gotland they say Vivil of Aikgard dug up his dead brother's silver one night and buried it again the next, and that not even his dog knows where.
On Gotland they say Hegbjorn of Aikgard spoke of forty marks and left fifteen. His kin have turned over half the farm. The Frisian who brought the word said the floor was all he knew.

On Gotland they say a Frisian who came as a dead man's messenger walked out to the old stones at Aikgard by night with a spade. There is a hole there now. His sail is known on every beach of the island.

At Paviken a new ship is home from the east: built with a dead man's silver, steered by his brother's son, a third of her a Frisian's. There is a Frisian booth on the beach. The old men say it will not last.

A Gotland ship in from the east road had Rhine wine aboard and a Frisian's tally stick beside her master's. They say his house has a booth on the beach at Paviken, which no outland man has had before.

A low back room in a harbour host's house, late afternoon light through a smoke hole: a grey, big-boned Gotlander of fifty-five under a sheepskin on a straw bed, gripping a Frisian merchant's hand; a folding scale and a yew stick on the chest beside him; the host in the doorway.

A harbour shore at dusk, wind off the land: a small pyre burning above the tide line, a Northman standing by it with his hood back; in front, on a table by the host's door, an open sea chest with a scale in a bronze case, a bag of weights, a comb and a rune-cut stick.

Aboard the small boat at sea on a grey, steady day: a broad dark-bearded Northman holding a short yew stick to the light and reading it with his thumb; a broad Frisian steersman looking away over the water; the folded scale on the thwart between them.

Paviken on a bright windy morning: a shingle beach, boat sheds, forge smoke, a half-planked hull on the slip; a Gotland shipwright in a leather apron who has just laid his adze on the strake, pointing inland up a stream.

Inside a Gotland long house at midday, hearth smoke under the roof: a heavy, careful farmer of fifty setting bread and an ale bowl before the merchant; by the open door a young widow in a strap dress with oval brooches, a small boy against her knee; through the door a storehouse on a stone footing and a tall picture stone.

A storehouse with its floor boards stacked against the wall, daylight from the south door: a hole under a lifted limestone slab, a bronze bowl with silver arm rings and a spilled bag of thin coins, many cut in half; the farmer kneeling on one side, his niece standing on the other, neighbours in the doorway.

A low Baltic skerry coast under a white sky, a light wind: a narrow six-oared boat lying across the bow of the small Frisian boat, oars held level; a fair-bearded Svea of thirty standing in her stern with one hand out, palm up.

A grassy slope above farms in late summer afternoon light, the sea a line behind: some sixty free men sitting in a ring with spears stuck upright behind them; in the middle a bronze bowl on a hide, the farmer on one side, the widow on the other, an old white-haired man with a staff, and the Frisian merchant standing alone.

A farm table by the open door at dusk: the farmer, his niece and his son of twenty-two leaning on their elbows; through the door, beyond a pasture fence, a ship setting of standing stones black against a yellow sky, sheep among them, and the merchant looking that way while nobody else does.

The stone ship at first light, mist in the pasture: the widow kneeling at a small folding scale set on a fallen stone, a pitch-sealed bronze bowl open beside her full of coiled silver rings; a fresh hole at the foot of the tall stern stone; her uncle a dark figure at the fence, hands on the top rail.

The farm table in early morning light: an empty pitch-smeared bowl, five small heaps of ring silver and three cakes of wax; the farmer standing behind it with earth on both knees and a spade against the door post; through the door, fresh-cut turf at the foot of a leaning stone.

The stone ship in the east pasture on a long northern summer evening: the merchant with one hand flat on the tall leaning stern stone, uncut turf at its foot; a Norse hand a few paces off with his arms folded; far behind, the farm's smoke, and a woman and a small boy at the fence.

The same stones on a moonless night, seen only by a lamp held under a cloak: two men lifting a pitch-sealed bronze bowl out of a hole at the stern stone, a spade stuck in the turf, the merchant looking over his shoulder toward one small red light at the farm.

Paviken beach on a clear early-autumn day: a new clinker ship drawn up on the shingle, her chequered sail spread to dry; a new timber booth above the tide line with skins stacked inside and a mark cut over its door; a young skipper, the widow with a tally stick and the old farmer with folded arms, waiting by a scale.
